pages.body:
You have probably heard parents or teachers say you must eat a balanced diet. But what does that actually mean? Think about the food you ate yesterday.

- Did your meals include foods from different food groups — carbohydrates, proteins, fats and vegetables?
- Have you ever seen a child whose stomach is swollen but whose arms and legs are thin? Or someone who cannot see properly at night?
- What do you think could be causing these conditions?

pages.title: What are food nutrients?
pages.body:
Food nutrients are the chemical substances in food that provide energy, support growth and repair, and regulate body processes. A balanced diet contains all nutrients in the right amounts. When any nutrient is missing or insufficient, a deficiency disease can develop.

> **DEFINITION** **Nutrient:** a chemical substance in food that the body needs for energy, growth, repair or regulation of body functions. **Deficiency disease:** a disease caused by the lack of a specific nutrient in the diet over a period of time. **Balanced diet:** a diet that contains all necessary nutrients in the correct amounts to keep the body healthy.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about a balanced diet is correct?
o: A balanced diet contains large amounts of protein and nothing else
A balanced diet must include only natural foods with no processed foods
A balanced diet contains all nutrients in the correct proportions to keep the body healthy
A balanced diet means eating the same meal every day
questions.e: Balanced diet: a diet that contains all necessary nutrients in the correct amounts to keep the body healthy.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The main food nutrients and their roles

pages.title: The main food nutrients and their roles
pages.body:
[[img:ikyf2yvg0]]

| **Nutrient** | **Role in the body** | **Main food sources in Ghana** |
|---|---|---|
| Carbohydrates | The body's main source of energy. Broken down to glucose, which fuels every cell. Simple carbohydrates (sugars) give quick energy; complex carbohydrates (starches) give longer-lasting energy. | Maize (kenkey, banku, tuo zaafi), yam, cassava, cocoyam, rice, millet, sorghum, bread, plantain |
| Proteins | Used to build and repair body tissues, make enzymes, hormones and antibodies. Every cell contains protein. | Meat (beef, mutton, poultry), fish (tilapia, herrings, tuna), eggs, milk, beans, groundnuts, soya, kontomire |
| Fatty acids (fats and oils) | Provide concentrated energy; help absorb fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K); form cell membranes; insulate the body; support brain development. | Palm oil, groundnut oil, coconut, oily fish (herrings, mackerel), nuts, avocado, shea butter |
| Vitamin A | Needed for healthy vision (especially in dim light), skin health, immune function and growth. | Palm oil, carrots, mango, papaya, eggs, liver, dark green vegetables |
| Vitamin C | Needed to make collagen (which holds skin, gums and blood vessels together); helps absorb iron; supports immune function. | Oranges, lemons, guavas, tomatoes, peppers, pineapple, fresh vegetables |
| Vitamin D | Needed for the body to absorb calcium and phosphorus; essential for strong bones and teeth. | Sunlight (main source); oily fish, eggs, liver, fortified foods |
| Iron (mineral) | Needed to make haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen around the body. | Liver, red meat, dark green leafy vegetables, legumes (beans), fortified cereals |
| Calcium (mineral) | Builds and maintains strong bones and teeth; needed for muscle contraction and nerve function. | Milk, cheese, yoghurt, sardines (with bones), dark leafy greens, beans |

questions.q: Which nutrient does the body use primarily as its main source of energy?
questions.e: Carbohydrates   The body's main source of energy.

questions.q: Which of the following is the main Ghanaian food source of Vitamin A?
questions.e: Eat vitamin A-rich foods: palm oil, carrots, eggs, liver, coloured vegetables and fruits.

questions.q: What is the role of iron in the human body?
o: To provide energy for daily activities
To make haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in red blood cells
To produce digestive enzymes in the stomach
questions.e: Iron (mineral)   Needed to make haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen around the body.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs correctly matches a nutrient to its food source?
o: Iron — liver and dark leafy greens
questions.e: Liver, red meat, dark green leafy vegetables, legumes (beans), fortified cereals

questions.q: Which nutrient is the main source of energy for the brain?
questions.e: Carbohydrates   The body's main source of energy.

questions.q: State the role of carbohydrates in the body and give four Ghanaian foods that are rich in carbohydrates.

parts.a: Carbohydrates are the body's main source of energy; they are broken down to glucose which fuels every cell. Foods: maize (kenkey, banku), yam, cassava, cocoyam, rice, millet, bread, plantain.

ideas.t: Carbohydrates are the main source of energy
They are broken down to glucose which fuels every cell
A food such as maize, kenkey, banku or tuo zaafi
Yam, cassava or cocoyam
Rice, millet, sorghum, bread or plantain

questions.q: Explain why protein is essential for children's growth. Which Ghanaian foods are good protein sources?

parts.a: Protein builds and repairs body tissues and every cell contains protein, so growing children need it. Good sources: meat, fish, eggs, milk, beans, groundnuts and soya.

ideas.t: Protein builds and repairs body tissues
Makes enzymes, hormones and antibodies
Every cell contains protein
Sources: meat, fish, eggs, milk, beans, groundnuts, soya

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Deficiency diseases: causes, symptoms, effects and prevention

pages.title: Deficiency diseases: causes, symptoms, effects and prevention
pages.body:
| **Disease** | **Nutrient lacking** | **Cause** | **Symptoms and effects** | **Prevention** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kwashiorkor | Protein | Diet contains enough calories (usually from starchy foods) but very little protein. Common in young children recently weaned onto a starchy diet. | Swollen abdomen (oedema), wasted and weak muscles, changes in skin and hair colour (reddish hair, pale skin patches), poor growth, reduced immunity, poor mental development | Eat protein-rich foods daily: meat, fish, eggs, beans, milk, soya. Breastfeed infants. Introduce protein-rich complementary foods on weaning. |
| Marasmus | All energy nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats) | Severe overall starvation — the body lacks almost all nutrients. | Extreme wasting of muscle and fat, the body looks like skin over bones, very low weight for age, weakness and apathy | Ensure adequate food intake of all nutrients. Address poverty and food insecurity. |
| Anaemia (iron-deficiency) | Iron | Insufficient iron in diet; sometimes caused by heavy blood loss or parasitic infections (e.g. hookworm). | Fatigue and weakness, pale skin and inner eyelids, breathlessness on exertion, dizziness, cold hands and feet, poor concentration | Eat iron-rich foods (liver, red meat, leafy greens, beans). Take iron supplements if prescribed. Treat underlying infections. |
| Night blindness | Vitamin A | Insufficient vitamin A causes the retina to fail in low light conditions. | Inability to see clearly in dim light or at night. If severe and untreated, can progress to complete blindness (xerophthalmia). | Eat vitamin A-rich foods: palm oil, carrots, eggs, liver, coloured vegetables and fruits. Take vitamin A supplements for young children. |
| Rickets | Vitamin D (and calcium) | Insufficient vitamin D, which prevents proper absorption of calcium, leading to soft weak bones. | Soft, weak and deformed bones (bowed legs, knock knees), pain in bones, poor growth, weak muscles, delayed tooth development | Get adequate sunlight daily. Eat vitamin D-rich foods: oily fish, eggs. Vitamin D and calcium supplements if needed. |
| Scurvy | Vitamin C | Diet lacking fresh fruits and vegetables for a prolonged period. | Bleeding and swollen gums, loose teeth, slow wound healing, bruising easily, joint pain, fatigue | Eat fresh fruits and vegetables daily: oranges, guavas, tomatoes, peppers, leafy greens. |

questions.q: A child has a swollen abdomen, wasted muscles and reddish hair. Which deficiency disease does this most likely indicate?
questions.e: Swollen abdomen (oedema), wasted and weak muscles, changes in skin and hair colour (reddish hair, pale skin patches), poor growth, reduced immunity, poor mental development   Eat protein-rich foods daily: meat, fish, eggs, beans,…

questions.q: A child has soft, bowed legs and poor bone development. Which nutrient deficiency is most likely responsible?
questions.e: Soft, weak and deformed bones (bowed legs, knock knees), pain in bones, poor growth, weak muscles, delayed tooth development   Get adequate sunlight daily.

questions.q: Night blindness is caused by a deficiency of which vitamin?
questions.e: Night blindness   Vitamin A   Insufficient vitamin A causes the retina to fail in low light conditions.

questions.q: Which deficiency disease is characterised by bleeding gums and slow wound healing?
questions.e: Bleeding and swollen gums, loose teeth, slow wound healing, bruising easily, joint pain, fatigue   Eat fresh fruits and vegetables daily: oranges, guavas, tomatoes, peppers, leafy greens.

questions.q: Marasmus differs from kwashiorkor in that marasmus is caused by:
o: Lack of protein only, while overall calorie intake is sufficient
Lack of vitamin A in the diet
Deficiency of all energy nutrients, resulting in severe starvation
questions.e: Marasmus   All energy nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats)   Severe overall starvation — the body lacks almost all nutrients.

questions.q: A farmer's child who eats mostly yam and cassava with very little fish or meat is at risk of developing:
questions.e: Kwashiorkor   Protein   Diet contains enough calories (usually from starchy foods) but very little protein.

questions.q: What is kwashiorkor? State its cause, three symptoms and two ways of preventing it.

parts.a: Kwashiorkor is a deficiency disease caused by a lack of protein in a diet that has enough calories from starchy foods. Symptoms: swollen abdomen, wasted weak muscles, reddish hair, pale skin patches, poor growth. Prevention: eat protein-rich foods such as meat, fish, eggs, beans and milk daily.

ideas.t: Protein is lacking while energy (starchy food) is enough
Swollen abdomen (oedema)
Wasted weak muscles
Changes in skin and hair colour
Prevention: eat protein-rich foods daily (meat, fish, eggs, beans, milk, soya)

questions.q: Explain why marasmus is more severe than kwashiorkor.

parts.a: Marasmus is caused by a lack of all energy nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins and fats) through severe starvation, so the body wastes away to skin and bones, while kwashiorkor is mainly a lack of protein.

ideas.t: Marasmus is a lack of all energy nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins and fats)
Severe starvation with extreme wasting of muscle and fat

questions.q: Describe the symptoms of anaemia and explain the role of iron in the body.

parts.a: Symptoms: fatigue and weakness, pale skin and inner eyelids, breathlessness, dizziness, cold hands and feet. Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen around the body.

ideas.t: Fatigue or weakness
Pale skin or breathlessness or dizziness
Iron makes haemoglobin
Haemoglobin in red blood cells carries oxygen

questions.q: Why does lack of Vitamin A lead to night blindness? Explain the connection between the vitamin and vision.

parts.a: Vitamin A is needed for healthy vision, especially in dim light. Without enough, the retina fails in low light, so the person cannot see clearly in dim light or at night.

ideas.t: Vitamin A is needed for healthy vision, especially in dim light
Without it the retina fails in low light so one cannot see at night

questions.q: State the symptoms of rickets and explain how sunlight helps prevent it.

parts.a: Rickets causes soft, weak, deformed bones (bowed legs, knock knees), bone pain and poor growth. Sunlight is the main source of vitamin D, which helps the body absorb calcium for strong bones.

ideas.t: Soft, weak, deformed or bowed bones
Sunlight is the main source of vitamin D
Vitamin D helps absorb calcium for strong bones

questions.q: Explain what scurvy is. Which foods prevent it and why?

parts.a: Scurvy is a deficiency disease caused by a lack of vitamin C, with bleeding swollen gums, loose teeth and slow wound healing. Fresh fruits and vegetables such as oranges, guavas, tomatoes and peppers prevent it because they contain vitamin C.

ideas.t: Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C
Bleeding gums, slow wound healing
Prevented by oranges, guavas, tomatoes or fresh vegetables
Because they contain vitamin C

questions.q: A student eats kenkey with stew every day but rarely eats meat, eggs or beans. Which deficiency disease might they develop over time? Explain your answer.

parts.a: Kwashiorkor (protein deficiency), because the diet has plenty of starchy food but very little protein.

ideas.t: Kwashiorkor or protein deficiency
Because the diet is starchy with little meat, eggs or beans

questions.q: Explain the difference between a deficiency disease and an infectious disease.

parts.a: A deficiency disease is caused by lack of a nutrient in the diet over a period of time (for example kwashiorkor); an infectious disease is caused by a pathogen such as a virus, which spreads from person to person.

ideas.t: A deficiency disease is caused by lack of a nutrient over time
An infectious disease is caused by a pathogen such as a virus and spreads

questions.q: A mother brings her two-year-old child to a clinic. The child was recently weaned from breastfeeding and now eats mostly banku with pepper soup and rarely gets fish or eggs. The child has a swollen belly, reddish hair and is not growing well. (a) Which deficiency disease does the child most likely have? (b) Which nutrient is lacking? (c) What specific foods would you recommend and why?

parts.a: (a) Kwashiorkor. (b) Protein is lacking. (c) Fish, eggs, beans, milk, meat and soya, because they are protein-rich foods that build tissues and prevent kwashiorkor.

ideas.t: (a) Kwashiorkor
(b) Protein is lacking
(c) Fish or eggs
(c) Beans, milk, meat or soya
Because they are rich in protein

questions.q: A survey of five families in a coastal fishing village shows that children who regularly eat fresh fish, eggs, palm nut soup and green vegetables are healthier than those who eat mainly gari and maize porridge. Explain which specific nutrients the healthier children are getting more of, and which deficiency diseases the others risk developing.

parts.a: The healthier children get more protein (fish, eggs), vitamin A (palm nut soup, vegetables), iron and vitamins from green vegetables. The others eating mainly gari and maize porridge risk kwashiorkor, night blindness, anaemia and scurvy.

ideas.t: Protein from fish and eggs
Vitamin A from palm nut soup and vegetables
Iron or vitamin C from green vegetables
Others risk kwashiorkor or other deficiency diseases

pages.title: Goitre and calcium deficiency
pages.body:
| **Condition** | **Nutrient lacking** | **Cause** | **Symptoms and effects** | **Prevention** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Goitre | Iodine | Too little iodine in the diet, which is common where the soil and water contain little iodine. | A swelling at the front of the neck where the thyroid gland becomes larger. In children it can slow growth and mental development. | Use iodised salt. Eat sea fish and other foods that contain iodine. |
| Weak bones and teeth | Calcium | Too little calcium in the diet, or too little vitamin D to help the body absorb it. | Bones become soft and break easily. In children the bones may bend, as in rickets. Teeth decay easily. | Eat milk, small fish eaten with their bones and green vegetables, and get some sunlight for vitamin D. |

> **Did you know?** Kwashiorkor is common in parts of Ghana, particularly during periods when families rely heavily on starchy staples like cassava and kenkey without adequate protein. Community health centres often provide nutrition counselling and supplementary feeding to prevent and treat this disease in young children.

> **Lesson 1 Assessment**

questions.q: What is goitre? State its cause and one way of preventing it.

parts.a: Goitre is a swelling at the front of the neck where the thyroid gland becomes larger. It is caused by too little iodine in the diet and can be prevented by using iodised salt or eating sea fish.

ideas.t: A swelling at the front of the neck
Caused by too little iodine
Prevention: iodised salt or sea fish

questions.q: State two effects of a lack of calcium in the body.

parts.a: Bones become soft and break easily. In children the bones may bend, as in rickets. Teeth decay easily.

ideas.t: Bones become soft or weak and break easily
Bones bend, as in rickets
Teeth decay easily

questions.q: Many people in a village far from the sea have a swelling at the front of the neck. Name the condition, the nutrient that is lacking and one cheap way the community can prevent it.

parts.a: The condition is goitre. The nutrient that is lacking is iodine. The community can prevent it cheaply by using iodised salt.

ideas.t: Goitre
Iodine is lacking
Use iodised salt or eat sea fish

pages.body:
In 2020, a new disease spread from one country to almost every country in the world within a few months. Schools closed, borders shut, and millions of people became ill. That disease was COVID-19. A few years before that, another disease, Ebola, caused a devastating outbreak in West Africa.

- What do you know about COVID-19 or Ebola? Where did you first hear about them?
- How do you think a disease can spread from one person to another without any physical contact?
- Why do you think some diseases become pandemics while others stay in one area?

pages.title: What is a virus?
pages.body: A virus is a microscopic organism that is smaller than a bacterium and can only reproduce inside the living cells of a host. Viruses cannot grow or reproduce on their own. Once inside a host cell, they hijack the cell's machinery to make copies of themselves, eventually bursting out and infecting more cells. This causes disease.

> **DEFINITION** **Virus:** a microscopic infectious agent that can only replicate (reproduce) inside the living cells of a host organism. Viruses cause viral diseases. **Viral disease:** a disease caused by a virus attacking and reproducing inside the cells of the body. **Epidemic:** a disease that spreads rapidly to many people within a community, region or country. **Pandemic:** an epidemic that has spread across multiple countries or continents, affecting a very large number of people worldwide. **Transmission:** the passing of a disease from one person, animal or place to another.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes how a virus differs from a bacterium?
o: Viruses can reproduce independently without any host
Viruses can only reproduce inside the living cells of a host organism
Viruses are killed by antibiotics, unlike bacteria
questions.e: A virus is a microscopic organism that is smaller than a bacterium and can only reproduce inside the living cells of a host.

questions.q: What makes a disease a pandemic rather than just an epidemic?
o: It affects animals as well as humans
It spreads to multiple countries or continents, affecting very large numbers of people worldwide
It causes more than 1,000 deaths in one country
It is caused by a virus rather than a bacterium
questions.e: Pandemic: an epidemic that has spread across multiple countries or continents, affecting a very large number of people worldwide.

questions.q: Define a virus. Explain how viruses reproduce and why they cause disease.

parts.a: A virus is a microscopic infectious agent smaller than a bacterium that can only reproduce inside the living cells of a host. It hijacks the cell's machinery to make copies, which burst out and infect more cells, causing disease.

ideas.t: A virus is a microscopic infectious agent smaller than a bacterium
It can only reproduce inside the living cells of a host
It hijacks the cell's machinery to make copies, then bursts out and infects more cells, causing disease

questions.q: State the difference between an epidemic and a pandemic. Give one example of each.

parts.a: An epidemic is a disease that spreads rapidly to many people within a community, region or country; a pandemic is an epidemic that has spread across multiple countries or continents. Example: Ebola (epidemic) and COVID-19 or H1N1 (pandemic).

ideas.t: An epidemic spreads rapidly to many people in a community, region or country
A pandemic spreads across multiple countries or continents
An example such as COVID-19 or H1N1

pages.title: Nature of viral diseases
pages.body:
| **Feature** | **Viral diseases** | **Bacterial diseases (for comparison)** |
|---|---|---|
| Cause | Viruses (not alive in the traditional sense; need a host to reproduce) | Bacteria (living single-celled organisms) |
| Treatment | Antiviral drugs (for some viruses); supportive care; vaccines prevent many viral diseases | Antibiotics are effective against bacteria |
| Antibiotics | Antibiotics DO NOT work against viral diseases | Antibiotics work against bacterial diseases |
| Spread | Mostly through droplets, aerosols, body fluids, or contaminated surfaces | Through similar routes plus water and food |
| Examples | COVID-19, Ebola, H1N1, measles, chickenpox, rabies, HIV | Cholera, tuberculosis, typhoid |

questions.q: Why are antibiotics not effective against viral diseases such as COVID-19?
o: Antibiotics have too many side effects to be used
Antibiotics kill bacteria but viruses are not bacteria and are not affected by antibiotics
Antibiotics have not been tested on viral diseases
Viral diseases are too mild to need antibiotic treatment
questions.e: Treatment   Antiviral drugs (for some viruses); supportive care; vaccines prevent many viral diseases   Antibiotics are effective against bacteria

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Viral Diseases: COVID-19, Ebola and H1N1 (part 3)

pages.body:
| **Disease** | **COVID-19** | **Ebola** | **H1N1 (Swine Flu)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pathogen (cause) | SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus | Ebola virus (Filovirus family) | Influenza A (H1N1) virus |
| First identified | 2019, Wuhan, China | 1976, Democratic Republic of Congo; major West Africa outbreak 2014-2016 | 2009, Mexico and USA |
| Mode of transmission | Respiratory droplets and aerosols when coughing, sneezing or talking; touching contaminated surfaces then touching face | Direct contact with blood or body fluids of an infected person or animal (bats, primates); contact with dead bodies of patients | Respiratory droplets from coughing or sneezing; touching contaminated surfaces |
| Spread (person to person, community to community, country to country) | Very high — spreads easily through air. Moved globally through international travel within weeks of first cases. | Lower than COVID-19 — requires direct contact with body fluids. Spread mainly in communities with limited healthcare, but crossed borders during 2014 outbreak. | High — spreads like seasonal flu. Moved globally through travel. Especially dangerous to young adults and children in 2009. |
| Main symptoms | Fever, dry cough, fatigue, shortness of breath, loss of smell and taste, sore throat, body aches | Sudden high fever, severe headache, muscle pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, bleeding from body openings, organ failure | Fever, cough, sore throat, runny nose, body aches, fatigue, vomiting, diarrhoea in some cases |
| Effects on the body | Infects lung cells, causing pneumonia in severe cases; can affect heart, kidneys and brain; can cause long-term symptoms (Long COVID) | Extremely severe; kills up to 90% of those infected in some outbreaks; causes catastrophic organ failure and internal bleeding | Usually causes mild-to-moderate flu; can be severe in elderly, pregnant women, young children and those with underlying conditions |
| Why declared a pandemic | Spread to over 190 countries within months of first cases (declared pandemic March 2020) | 2014-2016 outbreak declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern; affected multiple countries | Declared pandemic by WHO in June 2009 as H1N1 spread to over 70 countries within weeks |
| Prevention | Vaccination, face masks, physical distancing, hand hygiene, ventilation of indoor spaces, isolation of cases | Isolate patients, use PPE (gloves, gowns, goggles), avoid contact with body fluids, safe burial practices, vaccine available since 2019 | Vaccination (annual flu vaccine), face masks, hand hygiene, covering coughs and sneezes |

questions.q: COVID-19 is caused by which pathogen?
questions.e: Pathogen (cause)   SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus   Ebola virus (Filovirus family)   Influenza A (H1N1) virus

questions.q: Which of the following is the primary mode of transmission of Ebola?
o: Respiratory droplets from coughing and sneezing
Direct contact with the blood or body fluids of an infected person or animal
questions.e: Mode of transmission   Respiratory droplets and aerosols when coughing, sneezing or talking; touching contaminated surfaces then touching face   Direct contact with blood or body fluids of an infected person or animal (bats,…

questions.q: The 2009 H1N1 pandemic was caused by which type of virus?
questions.e: Pathogen (cause)   SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus   Ebola virus (Filovirus family)   Influenza A (H1N1) virus

questions.q: Which of the following symptoms is MOST distinctive of Ebola compared to COVID-19?
o: Bleeding from body openings and organ failure
questions.e: Main symptoms   Fever, dry cough, fatigue, shortness of breath, loss of smell and taste, sore throat, body aches   Sudden high fever, severe headache, muscle pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, bleeding from body openings, organ…

questions.q: What is contact tracing, and why is it important in managing an outbreak?
o: It involves treating all infected patients with the same medication to stop the spread
It is the process of identifying and monitoring all people who may have been exposed to an infected person, to break the chain of transmission
It means testing every person in a country for a disease
It involves quarantining everyone in a community when one case is found
questions.e: Mode of transmission   Respiratory droplets and aerosols when coughing, sneezing or talking; touching contaminated surfaces then touching face   Direct contact with blood or body fluids of an infected person or animal (bats,…

questions.q: Which organisation declared COVID-19 a pandemic in March 2020?
questions.e: Why declared a pandemic   Spread to over 190 countries within months of first cases (declared pandemic March 2020)   2014-2016 outbreak declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern; affected multiple countries  …

questions.q: During the Ebola outbreak in West Africa (2014-2016), safe burial practices were emphasised. Why?
o: Because the Ebola virus can spread through contact with deceased patients' body fluids
Because it is culturally disrespectful to touch a deceased person
Because Ebola spreads through the air around dead bodies
Because Ebola only infects people during funeral gatherings
questions.e: Prevention   Vaccination, face masks, physical distancing, hand hygiene, ventilation of indoor spaces, isolation of cases   Isolate patients, use PPE (gloves, gowns, goggles), avoid contact with body fluids, safe burial…

questions.q: Describe how COVID-19 is transmitted from person to person, from community to community, and from country to country.

parts.a: By respiratory droplets and aerosols when coughing, sneezing or talking, and by touching contaminated surfaces then the face. It spreads very easily through the air and moved between countries through international travel within weeks.

ideas.t: Respiratory droplets and aerosols when coughing, sneezing or talking
Touching contaminated surfaces then the face
It spreads between countries through international travel

questions.q: State four symptoms of COVID-19. Which two symptoms are particularly distinctive of COVID-19 and not common in other flu-like illnesses?

parts.a: Fever, dry cough, fatigue, shortness of breath, loss of smell and taste, sore throat, body aches. The distinctive ones are loss of smell and taste.

ideas.t: Four symptoms such as fever, dry cough, fatigue, sore throat, shortness of breath or body aches
Loss of smell
Loss of taste

questions.q: Describe the symptoms of Ebola and explain why it has such a high death rate compared to many other diseases.

parts.a: Sudden high fever, severe headache, muscle pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash and bleeding from body openings. It is extremely severe, causing catastrophic organ failure and internal bleeding, killing up to 90% in some outbreaks.

ideas.t: Sudden high fever, severe headache, muscle pain, vomiting or diarrhoea
Bleeding from body openings
Organ failure and internal bleeding make it very deadly

questions.q: Explain why Ebola requires different prevention measures from COVID-19. Compare the transmission routes of both diseases.

parts.a: Ebola spreads by direct contact with the blood or body fluids of infected people or animals and dead bodies, so it needs isolation, PPE and safe burials. COVID-19 spreads through droplets and aerosols in the air, so it needs masks, distancing and ventilation.

ideas.t: Ebola spreads by direct contact with blood or body fluids
So prevention is isolation, PPE and safe burial
COVID-19 spreads by droplets and aerosols in the air
So it needs masks, distancing or ventilation

questions.q: What is H1N1 and why was the 2009 H1N1 outbreak declared a pandemic?

parts.a: H1N1 (swine flu) is a disease caused by influenza A virus with fever, cough, sore throat and body aches. It was declared a pandemic by WHO in June 2009 because it spread to over 70 countries within weeks.

ideas.t: H1N1 (swine flu) is caused by the influenza A virus
It spread to over 70 countries within weeks
WHO declared it a pandemic in June 2009

questions.q: Explain why antibiotics cannot be used to treat COVID-19, Ebola or H1N1.

parts.a: Antibiotics kill bacteria, but these diseases are caused by viruses, which are not bacteria and are not affected by antibiotics.

ideas.t: Antibiotics work against bacteria
These diseases are caused by viruses, which are not affected by antibiotics

questions.q: What is a vaccine and how does it protect a person from a viral disease?

parts.a: A vaccine introduces a weakened or inactive form of a pathogen to stimulate the immune system before infection, so the body can fight the real virus; it prevents the disease rather than curing it.

ideas.t: A vaccine contains a weakened or inactive form of a pathogen
It stimulates the immune system before infection
So it prevents (rather than cures) the disease

pages.title: Roles in managing viral diseases
pages.body:
**Individual and community roles**
- Follow all public health guidelines (mask wearing, physical distancing, handwashing) consistently.
- Get vaccinated when a vaccine is available and recommended.
- Isolate yourself if you feel ill and seek medical care early.
- Report suspected cases to health authorities promptly.
- Avoid spreading misinformation; share only verified information from health authorities.
- Support and care for sick family members while taking precautions to avoid infection.
- Practise safe burial procedures during outbreaks of diseases like Ebola.

**Government and health authority roles**
- Establish and enforce public health measures (lockdowns, travel restrictions, quarantine) during outbreaks.
- Ensure testing, contact tracing and isolation facilities are available.
- Procure and distribute vaccines and medicines to the population.
- Train and equip healthcare workers with personal protective equipment (PPE).
- Communicate accurate and timely information to the public.
- Work with international organisations (WHO, CDC, Africa CDC) for coordinated response.
- Fund research into vaccines, treatments and outbreak preparedness.

> **Did you know?** During the COVID-19 pandemic, Ghana was among the first African countries to receive vaccines through the COVAX programme. The Ghana Health Service coordinated a national vaccination campaign. Despite challenges, Ghana managed to avoid the catastrophic death tolls seen in some countries, partly because of strong community health infrastructure.

> **Lesson 2 Assessment**

questions.q: A person suspects they have COVID-19. Which of the following actions is MOST important to take immediately?
o: Go to the market to buy medicine
Continue working to avoid missing income
Isolate yourself and contact a health worker
Take antibiotics prescribed by a pharmacist
questions.e: Isolate yourself if you feel ill and seek medical care early.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about vaccines is correct?
o: Vaccines cure a disease after the person is already infected
Vaccines work by introducing a weakened or inactive form of a pathogen to stimulate the immune system before infection
Vaccines replace the need for all other public health measures
Vaccines are only effective against bacterial diseases
questions.e: Balanced diet: a diet that contains all necessary nutrients in the correct amounts to keep the body healthy.

questions.q: State three things an individual should do to protect themselves and their community during a viral disease outbreak.

parts.a: Wear masks, keep physical distance and wash hands; get vaccinated; isolate if ill and seek care; report suspected cases; share only verified information.

ideas.t: Wear masks, keep physical distance and wash hands
Get vaccinated when a vaccine is available
Isolate if ill and seek medical care early
Report suspected cases to health authorities
Share only verified information

questions.q: Describe three actions a government should take during a viral disease epidemic.

parts.a: Enforce lockdowns, travel restrictions and quarantine; provide testing, contact tracing and isolation facilities; distribute vaccines and medicines; train and equip health workers with PPE; communicate accurate information; work with WHO and fund research.

ideas.t: Enforce public health measures such as lockdowns, travel restrictions and quarantine
Provide testing, contact tracing and isolation facilities
Procure and distribute vaccines and medicines
Train and equip health workers with PPE
Communicate accurate information to the public
Work with WHO and Africa CDC, and fund research

questions.q: A new viral disease has been reported in a border town in Ghana. Cases are increasing rapidly, and people are beginning to travel to other cities. (a) Using what you know about how viral diseases spread, explain how this disease could spread from the border town to Accra. (b) State four measures the Ghana Health Service should take immediately to contain the outbreak. (c) State two actions individuals in the border town should take.

parts.a: (a) It could spread through infected people travelling by road to other cities, carrying it by droplets, body fluids or contaminated surfaces. (b) The Ghana Health Service should isolate cases, trace contacts, test, communicate accurate information, give vaccines, and equip health workers with PPE.

ideas.t: People travel from the border town to Accra and carry the disease
It spreads through droplets, body fluids or contact
Isolate cases and trace contacts
Test and give accurate information
Provide vaccines or equip health workers with PPE

questions.q: A student tells her friend that she does not need to wash her hands because she has already received a COVID-19 vaccine. Do you agree with her reasoning? Explain why vaccination alone is not sufficient and what other measures should still be followed.

parts.a: I disagree. Vaccination does not give complete protection and does not replace other public health measures; she should still wash hands, wear masks, keep distance and ventilate.

ideas.t: Disagree: a vaccine does not replace other measures
She should still wash her hands
And wear masks, keep distance or ventilate rooms

pages.body:
| **Word** | **What it means** |
|---|---|
| Nutrient | A substance in food needed for energy, growth, repair or body regulation |
| Deficiency disease | A disease caused by the prolonged lack of a specific nutrient in the diet |
| Balanced diet | A diet containing all nutrients in the correct proportions for good health |
| Kwashiorkor | A protein deficiency disease causing swollen belly, wasted muscles and skin changes |
| Marasmus | Severe deficiency of all energy nutrients leading to extreme wasting |
| Anaemia | Deficiency of iron causing reduced haemoglobin and poor oxygen transport |
| Night blindness | Vitamin A deficiency causing inability to see clearly in dim or dark conditions |
| Rickets | Vitamin D (and calcium) deficiency causing soft, deformed bones in children |
| Scurvy | Vitamin C deficiency causing bleeding gums, slow wound healing and loose teeth |
| Virus | A microscopic agent that can only reproduce inside the living cells of a host |
| Viral disease | A disease caused by a virus infecting and reproducing within body cells |
| Epidemic | A disease that spreads rapidly to many people within a region |
| Pandemic | An epidemic that has spread across multiple countries or continents |
| Transmission | The passing of a disease from one person or organism to another |
| Vaccine | A preparation that stimulates the immune system to recognise and fight a pathogen |
| PPE | Personal Protective Equipment — protective clothing and gear worn to prevent infection |
| Isolation | Separating a sick person from healthy people to prevent disease spread |
| Contact tracing | Identifying and monitoring people who may have been exposed to an infected person |

questions.q: Which of the following statements about a balanced diet is correct?
o: A balanced diet contains large amounts of protein and nothing else
A balanced diet must include only natural foods with no processed foods
A balanced diet contains all nutrients in the correct proportions to keep the body healthy
A balanced diet means eating the same meal every day
questions.e: Balanced diet: a diet that contains all necessary nutrients in the correct amounts to keep the body healthy.

questions.q: Which nutrient does the body use primarily as its main source of energy?
questions.e: Carbohydrates   The body's main source of energy.

questions.q: Which of the following is the main Ghanaian food source of Vitamin A?
questions.e: Eat vitamin A-rich foods: palm oil, carrots, eggs, liver, coloured vegetables and fruits.

questions.q: What is the role of iron in the human body?
o: To provide energy for daily activities
To make haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in red blood cells
To produce digestive enzymes in the stomach
questions.e: Iron (mineral)   Needed to make haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen around the body.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs correctly matches a nutrient to its food source?
o: Iron — liver and dark leafy greens
questions.e: Liver, red meat, dark green leafy vegetables, legumes (beans), fortified cereals

questions.q: Which nutrient is the main source of energy for the brain?
questions.e: Carbohydrates   The body's main source of energy.

questions.q: State the role of carbohydrates in the body and give four Ghanaian foods that are rich in carbohydrates.

parts.a: Carbohydrates are the body's main source of energy; they are broken down to glucose which fuels every cell. Foods: maize (kenkey, banku), yam, cassava, cocoyam, rice, millet, bread, plantain.

ideas.t: Carbohydrates are the main source of energy
They are broken down to glucose which fuels every cell
A food such as maize, kenkey, banku or tuo zaafi
Yam, cassava or cocoyam
Rice, millet, sorghum, bread or plantain

questions.q: Explain why protein is essential for children's growth. Which Ghanaian foods are good protein sources?

parts.a: Protein builds and repairs body tissues and every cell contains protein, so growing children need it. Good sources: meat, fish, eggs, milk, beans, groundnuts and soya.

ideas.t: Protein builds and repairs body tissues
Makes enzymes, hormones and antibodies
Every cell contains protein
Sources: meat, fish, eggs, milk, beans, groundnuts, soya

questions.q: A child has a swollen abdomen, wasted muscles and reddish hair. Which deficiency disease does this most likely indicate?
questions.e: Swollen abdomen (oedema), wasted and weak muscles, changes in skin and hair colour (reddish hair, pale skin patches), poor growth, reduced immunity, poor mental development   Eat protein-rich foods daily: meat, fish, eggs, beans,…

questions.q: A child has soft, bowed legs and poor bone development. Which nutrient deficiency is most likely responsible?
questions.e: Soft, weak and deformed bones (bowed legs, knock knees), pain in bones, poor growth, weak muscles, delayed tooth development   Get adequate sunlight daily.

questions.q: Night blindness is caused by a deficiency of which vitamin?
questions.e: Night blindness   Vitamin A   Insufficient vitamin A causes the retina to fail in low light conditions.

questions.q: Which deficiency disease is characterised by bleeding gums and slow wound healing?
questions.e: Bleeding and swollen gums, loose teeth, slow wound healing, bruising easily, joint pain, fatigue   Eat fresh fruits and vegetables daily: oranges, guavas, tomatoes, peppers, leafy greens.

questions.q: Marasmus differs from kwashiorkor in that marasmus is caused by:
o: Lack of protein only, while overall calorie intake is sufficient
Lack of vitamin A in the diet
Deficiency of all energy nutrients, resulting in severe starvation
questions.e: Marasmus   All energy nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats)   Severe overall starvation — the body lacks almost all nutrients.

questions.q: A farmer's child who eats mostly yam and cassava with very little fish or meat is at risk of developing:
questions.e: Kwashiorkor   Protein   Diet contains enough calories (usually from starchy foods) but very little protein.

questions.q: What is kwashiorkor? State its cause, three symptoms and two ways of preventing it.

parts.a: Kwashiorkor is a deficiency disease caused by a lack of protein in a diet that has enough calories from starchy foods. Symptoms: swollen abdomen, wasted weak muscles, reddish hair, pale skin patches, poor growth. Prevention: eat protein-rich foods such as meat, fish, eggs, beans and milk daily.

ideas.t: Protein is lacking while energy (starchy food) is enough
Swollen abdomen (oedema)
Wasted weak muscles
Changes in skin and hair colour
Prevention: eat protein-rich foods daily (meat, fish, eggs, beans, milk, soya)

questions.q: Explain why marasmus is more severe than kwashiorkor.

parts.a: Marasmus is caused by a lack of all energy nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins and fats) through severe starvation, so the body wastes away to skin and bones, while kwashiorkor is mainly a lack of protein.

ideas.t: Marasmus is a lack of all energy nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins and fats)
Severe starvation with extreme wasting of muscle and fat

questions.q: Describe the symptoms of anaemia and explain the role of iron in the body.

parts.a: Symptoms: fatigue and weakness, pale skin and inner eyelids, breathlessness, dizziness, cold hands and feet. Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen around the body.

ideas.t: Fatigue or weakness
Pale skin or breathlessness or dizziness
Iron makes haemoglobin
Haemoglobin in red blood cells carries oxygen

questions.q: Why does lack of Vitamin A lead to night blindness? Explain the connection between the vitamin and vision.

parts.a: Vitamin A is needed for healthy vision, especially in dim light. Without enough, the retina fails in low light, so the person cannot see clearly in dim light or at night.

ideas.t: Vitamin A is needed for healthy vision, especially in dim light
Without it the retina fails in low light so one cannot see at night

questions.q: State the symptoms of rickets and explain how sunlight helps prevent it.

parts.a: Rickets causes soft, weak, deformed bones (bowed legs, knock knees), bone pain and poor growth. Sunlight is the main source of vitamin D, which helps the body absorb calcium for strong bones.

ideas.t: Soft, weak, deformed or bowed bones
Sunlight is the main source of vitamin D
Vitamin D helps absorb calcium for strong bones

questions.q: Explain what scurvy is. Which foods prevent it and why?

parts.a: Scurvy is a deficiency disease caused by a lack of vitamin C, with bleeding swollen gums, loose teeth and slow wound healing. Fresh fruits and vegetables such as oranges, guavas, tomatoes and peppers prevent it because they contain vitamin C.

ideas.t: Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C
Bleeding gums, slow wound healing
Prevented by oranges, guavas, tomatoes or fresh vegetables
Because they contain vitamin C

questions.q: A student eats kenkey with stew every day but rarely eats meat, eggs or beans. Which deficiency disease might they develop over time? Explain your answer.

parts.a: Kwashiorkor (protein deficiency), because the diet has plenty of starchy food but very little protein.

ideas.t: Kwashiorkor or protein deficiency
Because the diet is starchy with little meat, eggs or beans

questions.q: Explain the difference between a deficiency disease and an infectious disease.

parts.a: A deficiency disease is caused by lack of a nutrient in the diet over a period of time (for example kwashiorkor); an infectious disease is caused by a pathogen such as a virus, which spreads from person to person.

ideas.t: A deficiency disease is caused by lack of a nutrient over time
An infectious disease is caused by a pathogen such as a virus and spreads

questions.q: A mother brings her two-year-old child to a clinic. The child was recently weaned from breastfeeding and now eats mostly banku with pepper soup and rarely gets fish or eggs. The child has a swollen belly, reddish hair and is not growing well. (a) Which deficiency disease does the child most likely have? (b) Which nutrient is lacking? (c) What specific foods would you recommend and why?

parts.a: (a) Kwashiorkor. (b) Protein is lacking. (c) Fish, eggs, beans, milk, meat and soya, because they are protein-rich foods that build tissues and prevent kwashiorkor.

ideas.t: (a) Kwashiorkor
(b) Protein is lacking
(c) Fish or eggs
(c) Beans, milk, meat or soya
Because they are rich in protein

questions.q: A survey of five families in a coastal fishing village shows that children who regularly eat fresh fish, eggs, palm nut soup and green vegetables are healthier than those who eat mainly gari and maize porridge. Explain which specific nutrients the healthier children are getting more of, and which deficiency diseases the others risk developing.

parts.a: The healthier children get more protein (fish, eggs), vitamin A (palm nut soup, vegetables), iron and vitamins from green vegetables. The others eating mainly gari and maize porridge risk kwashiorkor, night blindness, anaemia and scurvy.

ideas.t: Protein from fish and eggs
Vitamin A from palm nut soup and vegetables
Iron or vitamin C from green vegetables
Others risk kwashiorkor or other deficiency diseases

questions.q: What is goitre? State its cause and one way of preventing it.

parts.a: Goitre is a swelling at the front of the neck where the thyroid gland becomes larger. It is caused by too little iodine in the diet and can be prevented by using iodised salt or eating sea fish.

ideas.t: A swelling at the front of the neck
Caused by too little iodine
Prevention: iodised salt or sea fish

questions.q: State two effects of a lack of calcium in the body.

parts.a: Bones become soft and break easily. In children the bones may bend, as in rickets. Teeth decay easily.

ideas.t: Bones become soft or weak and break easily
Bones bend, as in rickets
Teeth decay easily

questions.q: Many people in a village far from the sea have a swelling at the front of the neck. Name the condition, the nutrient that is lacking and one cheap way the community can prevent it.

parts.a: The condition is goitre. The nutrient that is lacking is iodine. The community can prevent it cheaply by using iodised salt.

ideas.t: Goitre
Iodine is lacking
Use iodised salt or eat sea fish

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes how a virus differs from a bacterium?
o: Viruses can reproduce independently without any host
Viruses can only reproduce inside the living cells of a host organism
Viruses are killed by antibiotics, unlike bacteria
questions.e: A virus is a microscopic organism that is smaller than a bacterium and can only reproduce inside the living cells of a host.

questions.q: What makes a disease a pandemic rather than just an epidemic?
o: It affects animals as well as humans
It spreads to multiple countries or continents, affecting very large numbers of people worldwide
It causes more than 1,000 deaths in one country
It is caused by a virus rather than a bacterium
questions.e: Pandemic: an epidemic that has spread across multiple countries or continents, affecting a very large number of people worldwide.

questions.q: Define a virus. Explain how viruses reproduce and why they cause disease.

parts.a: A virus is a microscopic infectious agent smaller than a bacterium that can only reproduce inside the living cells of a host. It hijacks the cell's machinery to make copies, which burst out and infect more cells, causing disease.

ideas.t: A virus is a microscopic infectious agent smaller than a bacterium
It can only reproduce inside the living cells of a host
It hijacks the cell's machinery to make copies, then bursts out and infects more cells, causing disease

questions.q: State the difference between an epidemic and a pandemic. Give one example of each.

parts.a: An epidemic is a disease that spreads rapidly to many people within a community, region or country; a pandemic is an epidemic that has spread across multiple countries or continents. Example: Ebola (epidemic) and COVID-19 or H1N1 (pandemic).

ideas.t: An epidemic spreads rapidly to many people in a community, region or country
A pandemic spreads across multiple countries or continents
An example such as COVID-19 or H1N1

questions.q: Why are antibiotics not effective against viral diseases such as COVID-19?
o: Antibiotics have too many side effects to be used
Antibiotics kill bacteria but viruses are not bacteria and are not affected by antibiotics
Antibiotics have not been tested on viral diseases
Viral diseases are too mild to need antibiotic treatment
questions.e: Treatment   Antiviral drugs (for some viruses); supportive care; vaccines prevent many viral diseases   Antibiotics are effective against bacteria

questions.q: COVID-19 is caused by which pathogen?
questions.e: Pathogen (cause)   SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus   Ebola virus (Filovirus family)   Influenza A (H1N1) virus

questions.q: Which of the following is the primary mode of transmission of Ebola?
o: Respiratory droplets from coughing and sneezing
Direct contact with the blood or body fluids of an infected person or animal
questions.e: Mode of transmission   Respiratory droplets and aerosols when coughing, sneezing or talking; touching contaminated surfaces then touching face   Direct contact with blood or body fluids of an infected person or animal (bats,…

questions.q: The 2009 H1N1 pandemic was caused by which type of virus?
questions.e: Pathogen (cause)   SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus   Ebola virus (Filovirus family)   Influenza A (H1N1) virus

questions.q: Which of the following symptoms is MOST distinctive of Ebola compared to COVID-19?
o: Bleeding from body openings and organ failure
questions.e: Main symptoms   Fever, dry cough, fatigue, shortness of breath, loss of smell and taste, sore throat, body aches   Sudden high fever, severe headache, muscle pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, bleeding from body openings, organ…

questions.q: What is contact tracing, and why is it important in managing an outbreak?
o: It involves treating all infected patients with the same medication to stop the spread
It is the process of identifying and monitoring all people who may have been exposed to an infected person, to break the chain of transmission
It means testing every person in a country for a disease
It involves quarantining everyone in a community when one case is found
questions.e: Mode of transmission   Respiratory droplets and aerosols when coughing, sneezing or talking; touching contaminated surfaces then touching face   Direct contact with blood or body fluids of an infected person or animal (bats,…

questions.q: Which organisation declared COVID-19 a pandemic in March 2020?
questions.e: Why declared a pandemic   Spread to over 190 countries within months of first cases (declared pandemic March 2020)   2014-2016 outbreak declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern; affected multiple countries  …

questions.q: During the Ebola outbreak in West Africa (2014-2016), safe burial practices were emphasised. Why?
o: Because the Ebola virus can spread through contact with deceased patients' body fluids
Because it is culturally disrespectful to touch a deceased person
Because Ebola spreads through the air around dead bodies
Because Ebola only infects people during funeral gatherings
questions.e: Prevention   Vaccination, face masks, physical distancing, hand hygiene, ventilation of indoor spaces, isolation of cases   Isolate patients, use PPE (gloves, gowns, goggles), avoid contact with body fluids, safe burial…

questions.q: Describe how COVID-19 is transmitted from person to person, from community to community, and from country to country.

parts.a: By respiratory droplets and aerosols when coughing, sneezing or talking, and by touching contaminated surfaces then the face. It spreads very easily through the air and moved between countries through international travel within weeks.

ideas.t: Respiratory droplets and aerosols when coughing, sneezing or talking
Touching contaminated surfaces then the face
It spreads between countries through international travel

questions.q: State four symptoms of COVID-19. Which two symptoms are particularly distinctive of COVID-19 and not common in other flu-like illnesses?

parts.a: Fever, dry cough, fatigue, shortness of breath, loss of smell and taste, sore throat, body aches. The distinctive ones are loss of smell and taste.

ideas.t: Four symptoms such as fever, dry cough, fatigue, sore throat, shortness of breath or body aches
Loss of smell
Loss of taste

questions.q: Describe the symptoms of Ebola and explain why it has such a high death rate compared to many other diseases.

parts.a: Sudden high fever, severe headache, muscle pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash and bleeding from body openings. It is extremely severe, causing catastrophic organ failure and internal bleeding, killing up to 90% in some outbreaks.

ideas.t: Sudden high fever, severe headache, muscle pain, vomiting or diarrhoea
Bleeding from body openings
Organ failure and internal bleeding make it very deadly

questions.q: Explain why Ebola requires different prevention measures from COVID-19. Compare the transmission routes of both diseases.

parts.a: Ebola spreads by direct contact with the blood or body fluids of infected people or animals and dead bodies, so it needs isolation, PPE and safe burials. COVID-19 spreads through droplets and aerosols in the air, so it needs masks, distancing and ventilation.

ideas.t: Ebola spreads by direct contact with blood or body fluids
So prevention is isolation, PPE and safe burial
COVID-19 spreads by droplets and aerosols in the air
So it needs masks, distancing or ventilation

questions.q: What is H1N1 and why was the 2009 H1N1 outbreak declared a pandemic?

parts.a: H1N1 (swine flu) is a disease caused by influenza A virus with fever, cough, sore throat and body aches. It was declared a pandemic by WHO in June 2009 because it spread to over 70 countries within weeks.

ideas.t: H1N1 (swine flu) is caused by the influenza A virus
It spread to over 70 countries within weeks
WHO declared it a pandemic in June 2009

questions.q: Explain why antibiotics cannot be used to treat COVID-19, Ebola or H1N1.

parts.a: Antibiotics kill bacteria, but these diseases are caused by viruses, which are not bacteria and are not affected by antibiotics.

ideas.t: Antibiotics work against bacteria
These diseases are caused by viruses, which are not affected by antibiotics

questions.q: What is a vaccine and how does it protect a person from a viral disease?

parts.a: A vaccine introduces a weakened or inactive form of a pathogen to stimulate the immune system before infection, so the body can fight the real virus; it prevents the disease rather than curing it.

ideas.t: A vaccine contains a weakened or inactive form of a pathogen
It stimulates the immune system before infection
So it prevents (rather than cures) the disease

questions.q: A person suspects they have COVID-19. Which of the following actions is MOST important to take immediately?
o: Go to the market to buy medicine
Continue working to avoid missing income
Isolate yourself and contact a health worker
Take antibiotics prescribed by a pharmacist
questions.e: Isolate yourself if you feel ill and seek medical care early.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about vaccines is correct?
o: Vaccines cure a disease after the person is already infected
Vaccines work by introducing a weakened or inactive form of a pathogen to stimulate the immune system before infection
Vaccines replace the need for all other public health measures
Vaccines are only effective against bacterial diseases
questions.e: Balanced diet: a diet that contains all necessary nutrients in the correct amounts to keep the body healthy.

parts.a: Wear masks, keep physical distance and wash hands; get vaccinated; isolate if ill and seek care; report suspected cases; share only verified information.

ideas.t: Wear masks, keep physical distance and wash hands
Get vaccinated when a vaccine is available
Isolate if ill and seek medical care early
Report suspected cases to health authorities
Share only verified information

questions.q: Describe three actions a government should take during a viral disease epidemic.

parts.a: Enforce lockdowns, travel restrictions and quarantine; provide testing, contact tracing and isolation facilities; distribute vaccines and medicines; train and equip health workers with PPE; communicate accurate information; work with WHO and fund research.

ideas.t: Enforce public health measures such as lockdowns, travel restrictions and quarantine
Provide testing, contact tracing and isolation facilities
Procure and distribute vaccines and medicines
Train and equip health workers with PPE
Communicate accurate information to the public
Work with WHO and Africa CDC, and fund research

(a) Using what you know about how viral diseases spread, explain how this disease could spread from the border town to Accra. (b) State four measures the Ghana Health Service should take immediately to contain the outbreak. (c) State two actions individuals in the border town should take.

parts.a: (a) It could spread through infected people travelling by road to other cities, carrying it by droplets, body fluids or contaminated surfaces. (b) The Ghana Health Service should isolate cases, trace contacts, test, communicate accurate information, give vaccines, and equip health workers with PPE.

ideas.t: People travel from the border town to Accra and carry the disease
It spreads through droplets, body fluids or contact
Isolate cases and trace contacts
Test and give accurate information
Provide vaccines or equip health workers with PPE

questions.q: A student tells her friend that she does not need to wash her hands because she has already received a COVID-19 vaccine. Do you agree with her reasoning? Explain why vaccination alone is not sufficient and what other measures should still be followed.

parts.a: I disagree. Vaccination does not give complete protection and does not replace other public health measures; she should still wash hands, wear masks, keep distance and ventilate.

ideas.t: Disagree: a vaccine does not replace other measures
She should still wash her hands
And wear masks, keep distance or ventilate rooms
